issues.item: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising Others' is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile and the trauma type. The other items center on childhood physical abuse, mistrust, touch-sensitivity, fragmented memory, guilt, and self-damage; obsessive worry about harm befalling loved ones points to a different threat theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' suggests a home-intrusion/security threat theme. In this profile, threat is otherwise expressed as interpersonal danger cues (unexpected touch, ominous silence) linked to caregiver abuse. Without matching appraisals or memory content about break-ins or external intruders, this item is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Calvin grew up in a working-class North American household where his stepfather ruled the apartment with a belt, a glare, and the kind of unpredictability that made the whole place feel dangerous before anything was said. As a boy, he learned to read the air for signs of what was coming, and even now, at 55, divorced and living alone above his small fashion studio, he still describes the old fear as if it were lodged in his muscles. The violence itself is not something he can tell as a clean story. When he tries, the details come in fragments: a hallway, the smell of beer, a hand rising too fast, his own mind going blank. Sometimes he can picture it, but it feels numb and unreal, as though it happened to someone else; other times he is flooded with guilt, convinced that he must have done something wrong to deserve it. That broken, uncertain way of remembering leaves him unsettled, and it feeds the private conclusion that he has permanently changed for the worse, that whatever happened to him never really ended and that his reactions now mean something is deeply wrong with him.  

That conviction shapes the way Calvin lives. He dwells on what his stepfather and, later in life, other people have done to him, replaying old slights and humiliations with a sharp, resentful edge, and he also turns the blame inward, spending long stretches of time asking himself what he should have done differently. Because he has come to believe people cannot be trusted, he watches everyone closely, including clients and coworkers in the studio, bracing for deception or cruelty. He feels on guard even inside his own home, and silence is especially hard for him: when the room goes quiet, he gets the uneasy sense that something dangerous is about to happen. His fear of becoming "crazy" makes the alarm feel even more ominous, as if the very fact that he is startled or uneasy is proof that he is losing his grip. That belief has made him hyperaware of bodily contact, and if someone brushes against him unexpectedly on the crowded subway, in a fitting room, or while pinning fabric on a model, he reacts with a jolt of alarm before he can stop himself.  

The memories and the threat feed each other in a way Calvin finds exhausting. When he is startled by a touch or finds himself straining against an unnerving silence at home, the old scenes come back in pieces, not as a coherent narrative but as flashes that carry the same sickening feeling of helplessness. Those fragments do not settle things; they make the danger feel current, and the current fear in turn scrambles the memory further. He notices that the more his body stays keyed up, the harder it becomes to hold the abuse in mind as one intelligible account. Instead, it returns as scattered sensations and visual scraps, and that disjointed recall deepens his belief that he is permanently altered and not thinking normally. When he catches himself unable to organize the past, he assumes the worst about his own mind.  

Over the years Calvin has built routines around that sense of threat. He avoids dreams by staying up too late, keeping the television on, and steering clear of the particular late-night hours and quiet Sunday afternoons that tend to bring on nightmares. He tells himself he is simply working, but the habits also keep him from being alone with the images long enough for them to form. The problem is that the avoidance has left the memories even less settled. Whole stretches of the childhood abuse remain unspoken and half-shaped, and when he does recall them, they arrive in a numb, detached way that prevents him from making sense of what happened. That lack of a coherent story gives his negative appraisals more room to grow: if he cannot explain the past, he concludes there must be something fundamentally damaged in him, and that he is still the kind of person who will be hurt or humiliated again. In turn, those appraisals keep him scanning for danger in the studio and at home, tightening his vigilance and making every unexpected touch, every pause in conversation, feel loaded.  

Lately the cycle has become harder to manage. At work he has begun avoiding meetings that drag into the evening, and he has turned down opportunities that would require him to stay late with others in the quiet studio, because the silence there feels oppressive and the risk of being surprised by touch or criticism seems too high. At home he keeps lights on and occupies himself with errands, sketches, and old grievances, trying not to be alone with the memories. But the more he ruminates on what others did to him and what he may have done wrong, the more certain he becomes that he is irreparably changed, mistrustful, and close to unraveling. By the time he sought help, it was because he had started waking already braced for danger, unable to relax in his own apartment or trust his own reactions, and he was frightened that if this continued he would either withdraw from everyone entirely or finally lose his mind.
